This is the question every working American should be asking—and the answer should concern everyone.
The 2026 Social Security Trustees Report, released this week, now projects that the retirement trust fund will be depleted in 2032, a full year sooner than forecast last year. That's just six years away.
Despite the headlines, Social Security isn't going away. Workers will keep paying payroll taxes, and benefits will continue to be issued. The problem is that once the trust fund runs out of reserves, the program can only pay out what it collects in real time—and that won't be enough to cover all promised benefits.
If Congress does nothing, beneficiaries could face an automatic 22% cut in payments.
That's a hard pill to swallow for millions of Americans who have spent decades contributing to the system with every paycheck. The promise was simple: pay in during your working years and receive benefits in retirement, supported by the next generation of workers.
But the math has changed.
Fewer workers are supporting a growing retiree population. Birth rates have fallen. Immigration has slowed. The system that once had a comfortable cushion is now under increasing strain.
Over the next ten years, Social Security is expected to pay out roughly $3.8 trillion more than it brings in. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have known this was coming for years, yet the problem remains largely unaddressed.
If you're in your 40s or 50s, this isn't some distant policy debate—it's a retirement issue. Plan as if a 22% benefit cut is possible, and hope Washington finally acts before that becomes reality.

Working hard should still get you somewhere.
That’s the part that strikes a nerve.
Most people aren’t asking for an easy life. They’re not trying to avoid responsibility, effort, or sacrifice.
They’re reacting to the feeling that the rules changed.
For decades, the deal seemed straightforward: work hard, live within your means, stay out of trouble, and you could build a stable life. Not necessarily wealthy. Not necessarily glamorous. Just stable.
Today, many people feel like they’re holding up their end of the bargain while stability keeps moving out of reach.
Housing costs more. Food costs more. Insurance costs more. Cars cost more. Childcare costs more.
Yet the answer is often the same: work harder.
That’s where the frustration comes from.
Of course personal responsibility matters. Work matters. Discipline matters. Choices matter.
But it’s reasonable to ask whether a full-time job should still provide a realistic path to basic stability.
Because when 40 hours a week only covers survival, something feels off.
That isn’t prosperity.
It’s spending your life buying back the next two weeks, one paycheck at a time.

An 85-year-old retiree relying on Social Security shouldn’t have to come up with $10,000–$15,000 every year just to stay in a house they already paid off decades ago.
Property taxes do help fund important community services. But they are far from the only source of government revenue.
Governments also collect income taxes, sales taxes, corporate taxes, tariffs, permit and licensing fees, tourism-related revenue, public land lease payments, investment returns, and income from natural resources. In 2025 alone, customs duties generated more than $210 billion for the United States.
The resources are there. The alternatives are there.
Meanwhile, many seniors are seeing their property tax bills climb year after year simply because their home value increased on paper—not because their retirement income increased.
A home’s value can surge over time. A Social Security check rarely keeps pace.
After spending a lifetime paying off a mortgage, no retiree should face the possibility of being priced out of their own home because of rising property taxes when governments have multiple other revenue streams available.
Strong schools and well-funded local services matter.
Making sure seniors can remain in their homes matters too.
A fair and balanced system should be capable of achieving both.
#PropertyTaxes #CostOfLiving #HousingAffordability #TaxFairness #WorkingClass #MiddleClass

Strong schools and well-funded local services matter.
Making sure seniors can remain in their homes matters too.
A fair and balanced system should be capable of achieving both.

An 85-year-old retiree relying on Social Security shouldn’t have to come up with $10,000–$15,000 every year just to stay in a house they already paid off decades ago.
Property taxes do help fund important community services. But they are far from the only source of government revenue.
Governments also collect income taxes, sales taxes, corporate taxes, tariffs, permit and licensing fees, tourism-related revenue, public land lease payments, investment returns, and income from natural resources. In 2025 alone, customs duties generated more than $210 billion for the United States.
The resources are there. The alternatives are there.
Meanwhile, many seniors are seeing their property tax bills climb year after year simply because their home value increased on paper—not because their retirement income increased.
A home’s value can surge over time. A Social Security check rarely keeps pace.
After spending a lifetime paying off a mortgage, no retiree should face the possibility of being priced out of their own home because of rising property taxes when governments have multiple other revenue streams available.
Strong schools and well-funded local services matter.
Making sure seniors can remain in their homes matters too.
A fair and balanced system should be capable of achieving both.
#PropertyTaxes #CostOfLiving #HousingAffordability #TaxFairness #WorkingClass #MiddleClass

You can support funding schools, roads, firefighters, and local services while still recognizing that the property tax system has a serious flaw.
An 85-year-old retiree living on Social Security shouldn't be forced to pay $10,000–$15,000 a year just to remain in a home they already own.
Yes, property taxes help fund essential services. But governments have many other sources of revenue besides taxing homeowners year after year.
They collect income taxes, sales taxes, corporate taxes, tariffs, licensing fees, permit fees, tourism revenue, public land leases, investment income, and revenue from natural resources. In 2025 alone, the U.S. collected more than $210 billion in customs duties.
The money exists. The options exist.
Yet many seniors on fixed incomes are watching their property tax bills rise simply because the market says their home is worth more—not because their income increased.
A home can double in value. A retiree's Social Security check usually doesn't.
No one who spent decades paying off a mortgage should risk being taxed out of their home in retirement while governments continue to have numerous alternative sources of revenue available.
Supporting schools and local services is important.
Protecting seniors from losing their homes is important too.
A fair system should be able to do both.

People working full-time are often told that if they're struggling financially, they should cut back on small comforts like streaming subscriptions, coffee runs, or eating out. Yet when massive corporations and billionaires benefit from billions in tax breaks, subsidies, and government incentives, it's framed as smart economics.
The reality is that financial hardship isn't caused by a few everyday purchases. It's driven by wages that fail to keep pace with inflation, soaring housing costs, and an economy where a growing share of wealth flows to executives, investors, and the ultra-rich.
Working families are expected to tighten their belts and do more with less, while some of the wealthiest companies on Earth continue to receive public support and special tax advantages.
Instead of blaming people who are struggling to get by, maybe we should be asking why so many resources are directed toward those who already have more than enough.

$300 in January 2000 has the same buying power as $595.60 today.
That's not an opinion. That's the official CPI Inflation Calculator — the same tool the government itself uses to measure inflation.
So ask yourself honestly: did your paycheck in 2000 nearly double by 2026?
For most working Americans, the answer is no. Wages crept up slowly while the actual cost of living nearly doubled in the background — rent, groceries, healthcare, gas, everything.
This is why $15/hour doesn't feel like progress anymore. This is why two incomes barely cover what one income used to. The dollar didn't just lose value — your paycheck lost ground every single year and nobody adjusted for it.

post_content:
A 3% raise doesn’t feel like much when the cost of living got a bigger bump than your paycheck.
That’s why workers tune out when companies talk about “competitive annual raises.”
If prices rise faster than your income, you’re not moving forward.
You’re just losing ground a little more slowly.
According to the BLS, real average hourly earnings fell 0.7% from May 2025 to May 2026. Paychecks got bigger in dollars, but buying power got smaller after inflation.
So when employers hand out 2%, 3%, or 4% raises and expect applause, people notice.
The grocery store noticed.
The landlord noticed.
The insurance company noticed.
The utility bill noticed.
Everyone got their increase except the person doing the work.
And somehow employees are supposed to celebrate a raise that barely keeps up with falling behind.
A raise only matters when it improves your quality of life.
Everything else is just a nicer-looking number on paper.

As more businesses embrace digital payments, self-checkout kiosks, and cashless policies, a growing debate is emerging: should cash always be accepted?
Supporters of cash say it remains essential for freedom, privacy, and accessibility. Not everyone has a bank account, credit card, smartphone, or reliable internet connection. Cash also provides a dependable way to pay when power outages, technical issues, or system failures disrupt electronic transactions.
Others favor the convenience of a cashless economy. Digital payments are often faster, easier to track, and more efficient for businesses. Companies can reduce cash-handling costs, lower theft risks, and streamline operations, while many consumers enjoy the simplicity of tapping a card or phone.
At its core, the discussion is about inclusion, choice, privacy, and resilience. As technology continues to reshape how we pay, many believe keeping cash as an option helps ensure that everyone can participate in everyday commerce—regardless of their circumstances.

Cash also provides a dependable way to pay when power outages, technical issues, or system failures disrupt electronic transactions.
Others favor the convenience of a cashless economy. Digital payments are often faster, easier to track, and more efficient for businesses. Companies can reduce cash-handling costs, lower theft risks, and streamline operations, while many consumers enjoy the simplicity of tapping a card or phone.
At its core, the discussion is about inclusion, choice, privacy, and resilience. As technology continues to reshape how we pay, many believe keeping cash as an option helps ensure that everyone can participate in everyday commerce—regardless of their circumstances.

The math feels a little off. 
For many families, the challenge isn't too many small purchases—it's housing costs, everyday expenses, and wages that haven't kept pace with the cost of living.
Working people keep hearing about sacrifice. At some point, it's fair to ask why the biggest conversations rarely start at the top.
Maybe the real debate isn't about coffee budgets. Maybe it's about affordability, wages, housing, and who benefits most from today's economy.

author: Thomas Crawford
comment_text:
While you follow the socialist party playbook 

1. Heightening Contradictions (Agitation)
Stemming from Marxist theory, this strategy focuses on exposing the gap between the working class and the owners of capital.
 The Method: Activists focus heavily on existing friction points—such as wage stagnation, inflation, housing costs, or corporate profits—to show the public that the current system cannot fix their problems.
 The Goal: To move people from passive dissatisfaction to active political grievance by demonstrating that their struggles are structural, not personal failures.
2. Vanguardism and Professional Organizers
Developed by Vladimir Lenin in his 1902 treatise What Is To Be Done?, this strategy argues that regular working-class citizens, left to themselves, will only fight for minor economic fixes (like better pay or shorter hours) rather than systemic change.
 The Method: A dedicated group of highly disciplined, politically educated organizers (the "vanguard") embeds themselves within community groups, unions, and social movements.
 The Goal: To steer local, everyday complaints toward a broader, unified push against the entire economic or governmental system.
3. Cultural Hegemony and Subversion
Italian theorist Antonio Gramsci argued in the 1920s and 1930s that a ruling class maintains control not just through laws and police force, but through "cultural hegemony"—dominating a society's values, media, education, and traditions.
 The Method: Instead of relying strictly on an overnight armed revolution, activists work to critique and alter the foundational cultural institutions of a society over time.
 The Goal: To challenge mainstream assumptions about capitalism, patriotism, and authority, creating an environment where radical systemic change feels natural and necessary to the public.

author: Phil Radford
comment_text:
The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), or Iran nuclear deal (2015), faced significant criticisms from the outset. These centered on its structure, scope, verification, and long-term effectiveness. While supporters viewed it as a pragmatic way to extend Iran’s nuclear “breakout time” (the time to produce enough fissile material for a weapon) from a few months to about a year through temporary restrictions and monitoring, opponents argued it was flawed and ultimately counterproductive. ￼
1. Sunset Clauses (Temporary Restrictions)
Many key limits on Iran’s nuclear activities were not permanent but expired after 10–15 years (e.g., centrifuge limits around 2025–2026, enrichment/stockpile caps by ~2030–2031). Critics argued this legitimized Iran’s enrichment program, allowed it to retain infrastructure and knowledge, and provided a “patient pathway” to a nuclear weapon once restrictions lifted—essentially kicking the can down the road rather than eliminating the threat. ￼
2. Not “Comprehensive” — Narrow Focus on Nuclear Issues
The deal primarily addressed uranium enrichment, centrifuges, the Arak reactor redesign, and some plutonium pathways but did not constrain:
•  Iran’s ballistic missile program (key delivery system for potential nuclear weapons).
•  Its support for regional proxies and militant groups (e.g., Hezbollah, Hamas).
•  Broader conventional military or destabilizing activities. ￼
Sanctions relief (including access to frozen funds and oil revenue) was seen as empowering the regime to fund these activities, regional expansion, and internal repression without sufficient reciprocal limits. ￼
3. Verification and Inspection Weaknesses
•  No “anytime, anywhere” inspections of military sites; a process allowed up to ~24 days’ notice for some suspect sites, potentially enabling concealment of small-scale or clandestine activities. ￼
•  The deal closed or limited aspects of the IAEA’s probe into Iran’s past weaponization work (PMD — Possible Military Dimensions), which critics said undermined trust in the program’s peaceful intent.
•  Iran has a history of non-compliance and undeclared activities; post-2018 developments (after U.S. withdrawal) showed accelerated enrichment, reduced inspector access, and advanced centrifuges. ￼
4. Sanctions Relief and Front-Loaded Benefits
Iran received significant, relatively immediate economic relief (billions in unfrozen assets, lifted oil/export sanctions) in exchange for reversible nuclear steps. Critics contended this enriched the regime (including the IRGC) without ironclad guarantees, and “snapback” sanctions mechanisms were cumbersome or politically difficult to enforce fully. The power imbalance favored Iran in some views, as U.S. withdrawal carried fewer direct costs than Iran’s potential isolation. ￼
5. Compliance and Long-Term Outcomes
•  Iran was largely in compliance initially (per IAEA), but the deal’s fragility showed after the 2018 U.S. withdrawal under Trump: Iran resumed higher enrichment (up to 60%+), expanded stockpiles, installed advanced centrifuges, and limited monitoring. Breakout time reportedly shrank dramatically (to weeks in later assessments). ￼
•  Revival efforts under Biden stalled amid Iran’s advances, regional conflicts, and demands. By the mid-2020s, Iran was described as a nuclear “threshold” state, closer to weapons capability than before the deal in some metrics. ￼
Other Criticisms
•  It was seen by some (e.g., Israel, Gulf states, U.S. conservatives) as appeasement that shifted regional power dynamics toward Iran.
•  In Iran, hardliners criticized concessions on sovereignty and restrictions.
•  Structural issues like reliance on executive agreements (bypassing full treaty ratification in the U.S.) made it vulnerable to changes in U.S. administrations. ￼
In summary, proponents highlighted verifiable short-term constraints and diplomacy over confrontation. Critics (who proved influential in U.S. policy) viewed it as a temporary delay that strengthened Iran’s economy and nuclear latency without addressing the regime’s broader behavior or ensuring permanent denuclearization. The deal’s collapse after 2018 accelerated Iran’s program, underscoring debates over whether better alternatives (stricter limits, broader scope, or maximum pressure) existed. Perspectives vary by political viewpoint, but the sunset provisions, narrow scope, and verification gaps remain core debated flaws.

The Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), or Iran nuclear deal (2015), faced significant criticisms from the outset. These centered on its structure, scope, verification, and long-term effectiveness. While supporters viewed it as a pragmatic way to extend Iran’s nuclear “breakout time” (the time to produce enough fissile material for a weapon) from a few months to about a year through temporary restrictions and monitoring, opponents argued it was flawed and ultimately counterproductive. ￼
1. Sunset Clauses (Temporary Restrictions)
Many key limits on Iran’s nuclear activities were not permanent but expired after 10–15 years (e.g., centrifuge limits around 2025–2026, enrichment/stockpile caps by ~2030–2031). Critics argued this legitimized Iran’s enrichment program, allowed it to retain infrastructure and knowledge, and provided a “patient pathway” to a nuclear weapon once restrictions lifted—essentially kicking the can down the road rather than eliminating the threat. ￼
2. Not “Comprehensive” — Narrow Focus on Nuclear Issues
The deal primarily addressed uranium enrichment, centrifuges, the Arak reactor redesign, and some plutonium pathways but did not constrain:
•  Iran’s ballistic missile program (key delivery system for potential nuclear weapons).
•  Its support for regional proxies and militant groups (e.g., Hezbollah, Hamas).
•  Broader conventional military or destabilizing activities. ￼
Sanctions relief (including access to frozen funds and oil revenue) was seen as empowering the regime to fund these activities, regional expansion, and internal repression without sufficient reciprocal limits. ￼
3. Verification and Inspection Weaknesses
•  No “anytime, anywhere” inspections of military sites; a process allowed up to ~24 days’ notice for some suspect sites, potentially enabling concealment of small-scale or clandestine activities. ￼
•  The deal closed or limited aspects of the IAEA’s probe into Iran’s past weaponization work (PMD — Possible Military Dimensions), which critics said undermined trust in the program’s peaceful intent.
•  Iran has a history of non-compliance and undeclared activities; post-2018 developments (after U.S. withdrawal) showed accelerated enrichment, reduced inspector access, and advanced centrifuges. ￼
4. Sanctions Relief and Front-Loaded Benefits
Iran received significant, relatively immediate economic relief (billions in unfrozen assets, lifted oil/export sanctions) in exchange for reversible nuclear steps. Critics contended this enriched the regime (including the IRGC) without ironclad guarantees, and “snapback” sanctions mechanisms were cumbersome or politically difficult to enforce fully. The power imbalance favored Iran in some views, as U.S. withdrawal carried fewer direct costs than Iran’s potential isolation. ￼
5. Compliance and Long-Term Outcomes
•  Iran was largely in compliance initially (per IAEA), but the deal’s fragility showed after the 2018 U.S. withdrawal under Trump: Iran resumed higher enrichment (up to 60%+), expanded stockpiles, installed advanced centrifuges, and limited monitoring. Breakout time reportedly shrank dramatically (to weeks in later assessments). ￼
•  Revival efforts under Biden stalled amid Iran’s advances, regional conflicts, and demands. By the mid-2020s, Iran was described as a nuclear “threshold” state, closer to weapons capability than before the deal in some metrics. ￼
Other Criticisms
•  It was seen by some (e.g., Israel, Gulf states, U.S. conservatives) as appeasement that shifted regional power dynamics toward Iran.
•  In Iran, hardliners criticized concessions on sovereignty and restrictions.
•  Structural issues like reliance on executive agreements (bypassing full treaty ratification in the U.S.) made it vulnerable to changes in U.S. administrations. ￼
In summary, proponents highlighted verifiable short-term constraints and diplomacy over confrontation. Critics (who proved influential in U.S. policy) viewed it as a temporary delay that strengthened Iran’s economy and nuclear latency without addressing the regime’s broader behavior or ensuring permanent denuclearization. The deal’s collapse after 2018 accelerated Iran’s program, underscoring debates over whether better alternatives (stricter limits, broader scope, or maximum pressure) existed. Perspectives vary by political viewpoint, but the sunset provisions, narrow scope, and verification gaps remain core debated flaws.

President Obama's Iran nuclear deal (JCPOA) was valuable primarily because it verifiably cut off all of Iran's pathways to developing a nuclear weapon. From 1998 to 2013 (right before the bulk of the ACA took effect) total healthcare costs were increasing at 2.57% per year over inflation. From 2013 to 2025 they have been increasing at 2.40%. 1. Washington governor’s race (Chris Gregoire vs. Dino Rossi, 2004):

* It is true that previously uncounted ballots were discovered during the recount process, and administrative errors in King County became highly controversial. Hundreds of ballots that had been mistakenly rejected or not included were eventually counted.  
* However, there is no verified evidence that boxes of ballots were found in an election worker’s trunk weeks later and proven to have changed the election outcome. The election was extensively litigated and recounted, and Gregoire ultimately won by 129 votes.

* In April 2026, a box of ballots was indeed reported found near a dumpster behind a Renton strip mall.  
* But reports indicate they were largely unopened, unvoted, and from multiple past elections, and investigators had not concluded they were fraudulent votes or evidence of election tampering.  

3. Los Angeles mayoral race and Nithya Raman:

* California counts ballots for weeks after Election Day, so candidates can move up or down as late ballots are processed. That is normal and legal.  
* There is no evidence that 40,000 mystery ballots from Skid Row appeared and were 100% for Raman. No official results support that claim.  
* Claims that homeless residents were paid $5 to vote for Raman stem from a handful of social media videos and remain unsubstantiated. Journalists and election experts found no evidence of a widespread vote-buying scheme capable of altering the election.  

Bottom line: Administrative mistakes and unusual incidents involving ballots have happened and deserve investigation. author: Juan Carlos Centeno Vazquez
comment_text:
Congresswoman Jayapal, thank you for your unwavering commitment to Dreamers. Your advocacy has been a vital voice for our community for years. However, we have to address a difficult truth: after 14 years of focusing on the same 'Dreamer-only' legislative strategies, we are still waiting for a permanent solution. Repeating the same approach that has stalled for two decades is no longer enough to protect the millions of families currently in limbo.
My advocacy is deeply personal: my parents worked in this country for over 25 years and passed away without ever achieving the legal status they earned. They didn’t have a DACA permit, and they weren’t the 'professional' success stories often highlighted in these debates, but they were the backbone of our community. I don't want to see another generation lose that time waiting for a bill that is stuck in a cycle of partisan gridlock.
We need to evolve our strategy. The Dignity Act (H.R. 4393) is the first piece of legislation in years that has successfully built a truly bipartisan coalition, including an even split of 20 Democratic and 20 Republican co-sponsors and an official endorsement from the Problem Solvers Caucus. It is a comprehensive framework that provides an earned, legal path for both Dreamers and the long-term undocumented residents who have been ignored for far too long. Please use your influence to help champion this bipartisan path. Our community is tired of the anniversary rhetoric—we are ready for the permanent, bipartisan results that your leadership could help us achieve.

Juan,

How fair is it to my wife, who followed every law and every requirement of the U.S. immigration system?

When I was medically evacuated from Tokyo to California, I spent over a year in the hospital before retiring from the Air Force after 16 years of service. My wife and I had been married since 1998 in Japan, yet we still had to endure separation and wait for the legal immigration process to run its course.

Millions of families have done the same thing. They filled out the paperwork, paid the fees, attended the interviews, followed the rules, and waited patiently for approval.

When politicians demand special treatment for those who entered illegally, they rarely explain how that is fair to the people who respected U.S. law from the beginning. Compassion is important, but so is fairness.

The immigration debate cannot ignore the sacrifices made by legal immigrants and American families who followed the process, even when it meant years of separation and hardship. Rewarding those who bypassed the system sends a message to lawful immigrants that their patience, sacrifice, and respect for the law mattered less than simply crossing the border.

My wife earned her place here legally. So did countless others. Their stories deserve to be remembered too.

What has been most difficult is not just the shooting itself, but the lack of visible community support afterward.
Support matters. A phone call matters. A visit matters. A public statement matters. Asking, "How can we help?" matters.
When a nonprofit organization serving families, children, seniors, veterans, and individuals experiencing housing instability is impacted by violence, the community should come together. 
Support from town officials, community leaders, businesses, churches, civic organizations, and residents can make a tremendous difference.
Support is not about money. It is about showing up. It is about letting those affected know they are not alone. It is about advocating for justice, sharing information, checking in on victims, and standing united against violence.
In times of tragedy, people should not have to ask their community to care. The community should care enough to show up on its own.
That is the support we needed. That is the support we still need.

I am a person of reason and empathy, which is why I find it difficult to understand what happened after our transitional home—
Sage and Sweetgrass at the Bradshaw House Inc. , the only program of its kind in Ahoskie—was riddled with bullets and our beloved 5-year-old American Bully, Dior, was killed by a stray bullet.
The Ahoskie Police Department responded, and for that we are grateful.
 However, I believe that when a tragedy impacts a family, a nonprofit organization, or a business in our community, town leaders should rally around those affected and show support.
It should not be the responsibility of the victim to make phone calls explaining what happened or asking for help. 
There should be follow-up visits, advocacy, and outreach. Community leaders should check on those impacted, offer resources, and help ensure their voices are heard.
I also believe incidents of this magnitude deserve broader awareness. Media outlets should be notified, public officials should speak out against the violence, and social media should be used to keep the community informed and engaged.
When gun violence strikes a home filled with families, children, and vulnerable individuals, and a life is lost—even the life of a beloved family pet—it should matter to the entire community. 
Communities grow stronger when they stand together, not just during celebrations, but also during moments of tragedy.
We are still seeking accountability for the June 13, 2026 shooting at Sage & Sweetgrass at the Bradshaw House Inc. We remain committed to our mission of housing hope, not violence, and we hope our community will continue to stand with us as we seek justice for Dior and safety for all.

Another Success Story at Sage & Sweetgrass at the Bradshaw House Inc. 
A young lady who recently started a new job as a manager and is preparing to move to a new city in the coming weeks experienced unexpected car trouble. Concerned about getting to work, she reached out to Sage and Sweetgrass at the Bradshaw House Inc. for assistance.
Derrick went over to assess the vehicle, identified the issue, and we immediately ordered the necessary part. Since the repair could not be completed the same day, Sage & Sweetgrass at the Bradshaw House Inc. provided her with a vehicle to drive so she would not miss work while waiting for the part to arrive.
At Sage & Sweetgrass at the Bradshaw House Inc., we understand that reliable transportation is often the key to maintaining employment and achieving long-term stability. We are proud to support individuals as they work toward their goals and build brighter futures.
Congratulations to the young lady on her new management position and their upcoming move! We are proud of this young lady & her hard work and wish her continued success.

post_content:
These aren’t my words but they are very well said & I wanted to share them….
“We put on this uniform without ever asking which day will be the last.
We walk through terminals as if time is endless—never knowing when it will be the final boarding, the last laugh on the jumpseat, the last story shared somewhere above the clouds.
The smallest moments never feel like goodbyes…
until they are.
A plastic cup handed to a child.
A quiet smile to a stranger.
A routine flight that was never meant to be anything more than ordinary.
We leave home believing we’ll return—
never imagining that, somewhere across the world, a phone will ring…
and a family’s life will be forever divided into before and after.
A voice on the other end delivering the words no one is ever ready to hear:
they’re not coming home this time.
Tonight, my heart carries the weight of every life touched by the tragedy of Air Canada Flight 8646—
the crew, the passengers, air traffic control, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey staff,
and the families now left to hold what remains.
There are no right words for a loss like this—only silence, grief, and remembrance.
May your final journey be gentle.
May the skies hold you softly.
May you be carried home on endless tailwinds.
We may wear different uniforms…
but this pain, this love, this bond—we all share it.
Forever #UnitedByWings”

post_content:
These aren’t my words but they are very well said & I wanted to share them….
“We put on this uniform without ever asking which day will be the last.
We walk through terminals as if time is endless—never knowing when it will be the final boarding, the last laugh on the jumpseat, the last story shared somewhere above the clouds.
The smallest moments never feel like goodbyes…
until they are.
A plastic cup handed to a child.
A quiet smile to a stranger.
A routine flight that was never meant to be anything more than ordinary.
We leave home believing we’ll return—
never imagining that, somewhere across the world, a phone will ring…
and a family’s life will be forever divided into before and after.
A voice on the other end delivering the words no one is ever ready to hear:
they’re not coming home this time.
Tonight, my heart carries the weight of every life touched by the tragedy of Air Canada Flight 8646—
the crew, the passengers, air traffic control, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey staff,
and the families now left to hold what remains.
There are no right words for a loss like this—only silence, grief, and remembrance.
May your final journey be gentle.
May the skies hold you softly.
May you be carried home on endless tailwinds.
We may wear different uniforms…
but this pain, this love, this bond—we all share it.
Forever #UnitedByWings”
author: Mary Kay Hill
comment_text:
This is so beautiful, Nancy.
You always have such insightful words to share.
I flew for DAL for 42 years, and I always wondered what my fate would be:
Would I die in a crash?
Would I be severely injured in a crash?
Would that terrible tragedy never happen to me?
Now I’m retired for four and a half years and I know my fate from that worry.
While we never know our ultimate fate as to when/how we will cross to the other side. I am grateful that it wasn’t in a plane crash.
Prayers of safety for you, Nancy, and my many other FA friends still working.

post_content: We put safety first, we are the frontline to any problems in the cabin during flight, we serve food and drinks in both cabins, our small planes feed the mainline. Yet somehow we are not paid a living wage. Our trip extended past midnight into a day off— no extra pay unless we arrive after 2am. When passengers are boarding the plane— per diem pay only ($2 & change) until the door is closed and brakes released. We’ve been told that to pay us more would put the company out of business… hardly. We are part of Air Group that has purchased another airline and reached a contract with their flight attendants that pays them a living wage. Now it’s our turn, it’s time to “DO THE RIGHT THING”!! #contract #afa #flightattendant #travel #airlineindustry

Base closures are a way of corporate aviation— doesn’t mean I have to like it. It’s painful, it’s scary, your life is turned upside down and no one in charge seems to really care. Bottom line is the buck. Always. So I cherish these moments, try to keep my quivering chin up. Immensely grateful for an amazing crew on a long four day! Cherry on top was Reed earning his fourth stripe to officially become a captain— our little boy is all growed up!! People keep asking me what I’m going to do… what does one do at 61, when they’ve already started over late in the game? So unemployment it will be for the summer, reset my brain & my heart, hope that a path forward reveals itself. My parents didn’t raise no cream puff, I’ll survive. But I’m awfully tired of surviving… living in peace sure would be nice. #livewell #crewlife #aviation #travel #stewardess

post_content: Taking a moment to give a huge thank you to our pilots! Pat & Reed were amazing yesterday— they kept us safe, our passengers informed (even in the midst of chaos), all while handling some very tricky flying. I experienced some of the most harsh turbulence ever in my 37 industry years, it was not enjoyable to say the least! But they kept us safe, put the plane on the ground. Repeatedly. Yes, it’s their job, but how often do you think about the skill it takes to handle flying a jet? It takes a lot of skill & a very cool demeanor. These guys are my heroes & I will continue to harass them, joke with them, all the while singing their praises as they keep us safe… and alive!

post_content:
Let me say this loud so nobody in the back can pretend they didn’t hear it.
The people crying that they “need their own halftime show” are the same kind of people who once thought they needed their own water fountains.
Same mindset. Same insecurity. Same entitlement. Same ugly need to separate themselves and feel more important than everyone else.
And let’s stop pretending this just randomly showed up. It didn’t. This got worse. Way worse. The minute Trump took office.
Because suddenly people felt bold again. They stopped whispering. They stopped hiding it. They stopped pretending they were embarrassed by their small thinking.
They felt safe saying it out loud. Safe being selfish. Safe being cruel. Safe demanding everything revolve around them.
He didn’t invent that mentality. This country has always had it. But he gave it permission. He gave it a microphone. He made it loud. He made people think their worst instincts were something to be proud of.
Now every time something celebrates someone different, someone brown, someone Black, someone queer, someone not them, they act like it’s an attack. Like equality is theft. Like someone else being seen somehow erases them.
That is the exact same energy that built segregated water fountains. The same thinking that said separate but equal. The same thinking that needed its own door, its own section, its own everything just to feel superior.
Think about how fragile that is.
Imagine needing your own fountain just to feel important. Now imagine being so threatened by a halftime show that you melt down like the world ended.
It’s the same thing. Just dressed up differently.
They scream about freedom while begging for separation. They scream about unity while demanding division. They scream about fairness while asking for special treatment.
It’s backwards. It’s exhausting. And it’s embarrassing.
You don’t need your own halftime show. You don’t need your own anything. You’re not being erased. You’re just not the center of attention for five minutes and your ego can’t handle it.
That’s not oppression.
That’s insecurity.
And history has already shown us what happens when insecure people start demanding separation to feel powerful. We’ve seen that movie before. It never ends well.
Same mindset. Different decade. Louder excuses.
And ever since Trump took office, they stopped pretending they were ashamed of it. They wear it proudly now.
That’s the part that should scare everyone.
Because nothing is more dangerous than people who mistake their smallness for strength.

post_content:
Can’t take credit for this but it is spot on!
Life of a Flight Attendant:
We never say I'm flying to London , we
say I HAVE London! 
We trade too, and say things like "Who wants Istanbul? I need Dubai”…Yes, like we own the whole damn world! 
We drink soup from paper cups like it's coffee in the middle of the night, we use military time to set our alarm, we can finish a meal in 30 seconds standing up...behind a curtain & in between meal service & clearance. 
We hate when you stand up after the plane lands, we laugh when you clap after the plane lands. 
We love when you thank us. 
Aircraft is for Flight Attendants, Airplane is for passengers. 
We talk in dates even if it’s just the next day. 
We never know what day it is but we remember what supermarket is closest to our hotel. 
We are the best packers and can find anything we see in a magazine in the world, clothes, furniture,the best restaurants, best hotels, sightseeing excursions, etc... 
We may especially have loved working with someone specifically without knowing that person's name or if we will ever fly together again. 
“4L” or “1R” may be our names for the day. 
We all have woken up in the middle of the night with a mini heart attack forgetting where we are. We see beautiful places but no one to share the moment with.
We are always, always alone in a crowd…
#UnitedByWings

post_content:
Can’t take credit for this but it is spot on!
Life of a Flight Attendant:
We never say I'm flying to London , we
say I HAVE London! 
We trade too, and say things like "Who wants Istanbul? I need Dubai”…Yes, like we own the whole damn world! 
We drink soup from paper cups like it's coffee in the middle of the night, we use military time to set our alarm, we can finish a meal in 30 seconds standing up...behind a curtain & in between meal service & clearance. 
We hate when you stand up after the plane lands, we laugh when you clap after the plane lands. 
We love when you thank us. 
Aircraft is for Flight Attendants, Airplane is for passengers. 
We talk in dates even if it’s just the next day. 
We never know what day it is but we remember what supermarket is closest to our hotel. 
We are the best packers and can find anything we see in a magazine in the world, clothes, furniture,the best restaurants, best hotels, sightseeing excursions, etc... 
We may especially have loved working with someone specifically without knowing that person's name or if we will ever fly together again. 
“4L” or “1R” may be our names for the day. 
We all have woken up in the middle of the night with a mini heart attack forgetting where we are. We see beautiful places but no one to share the moment with.
We are always, always alone in a crowd…
#UnitedByWings

Entrepreneurship changed the trajectory of his family’s life.
That belief is not theoretical for Thomas U. Kim. It is personal. And it is one of the reasons we are so excited to welcome him as the new Executive Director of SCORE.
Thomas has seen firsthand how access to guidance, accountability, and opportunity can transform a future. Now, he brings that lived understanding to the nation’s largest network of volunteer business mentors.
With more than 20 years of senior leadership experience across nonprofit, government, and private sector roles, Thomas is a seasoned transformation leader. He is also a decorated U.S. Army combat veteran and a strategic operator known for aligning vision with execution, strengthening performance, and driving sustainable growth.
His appointment comes at a pivotal moment as SCORE continues to foster vibrant small business communities through mentoring and education nationwide. Thomas combines operational expertise with a values-driven approach, positioning us to expand our impact and serve even more entrepreneurs.
Please join us in welcoming Thomas to the SCORE community. The next chapter starts now. #SOARwithSCORE

I think it's amazing that Michigan is trying to get the death with dignity law passed. Dr. Kevorkian was an amazing man and stood his ground helping patients die peacefully and on their terms.
The fact that people say hospice already provides this care, hasn't got a clue. Palliative care is completely different, it's allowing you to be so drugged up you're not even awake. Great way to spend your last time on earth with your loved ones. Imagine them being late for a dose of morphine and now that terminally ill patient is in unbearable pain and crying out for help. Where is a person's dignity in that?!?
How can anyone NOT support this but would like to give their damn animal more dignity than a human is beyond me. We can allow animals to be "put down" so they don't suffer. Humans should get the same dignity in their own life and more so than animals.
People think you can't back out once you decide, that's also FALSE. If anyone has actually looked into it, there is a prescription that has to be taken by the patient. The patient can decide not to take it, the patient could also even decide not to fill said prescription. 
I don't give a rats ass politics and religion set aside, nobody should ever have to watch or hear a loved one in unbearable pain their last moments on earth or in such a vegetative state they can't even spend quality time with loved ones. Nobody is playing "God" the person is deciding to choose their last moments in life to still be in comfort. 
I can only hope that if my time ever comes, I will be able to choose the outcome. 
#deathwithdignity #mybodymychoices #passthislaw #choices

​Today, we observe Juneteenth—a day that honors the liberation of our ancestors and the resilience of the human spirit. As we reflect on 1865, we must confront the reality of 2026. The struggle for constitutional, human, and civil rights did not end with the arrival of news in Galveston; it remains an ongoing, daily battle.

We know that our story doesn't end in struggle; it ends in power, it ends in purpose, and ultimately, it ends in victory.
​Through Heartbeat Movement Inc, we remain committed to reporting the truth and standing on the front lines. We will be heard. We are the flames. This is our time, and we will rise again—not because it was easy, but because it was destined.

In 1776, 
the institution of slavery was legal and widespread across all 13 American colonies. 

Approximately 500,000 African Americans lived in the colonies, with enslaved individuals making up roughly 90% of this population. 
**The economy and society were deeply intertwined with human chattel slavery** …. 

The Contradiction of LibertyWhen the Continental Congress declared independence from Great Britain in 1776, they proclaimed that "all men are created equal". However, this did not apply to enslaved African Americans. 

Thomas Jefferson, himself an enslaver, drafted a passage in the Declaration of Independence criticizing the British king for the slave trade, 
but the Continental Congress removed it due to pressure from Southern and Northern delegates who had financial stakes in the institution. 

The British "Liberty to Slaves" PromiseDuring the Revolutionary War, 
the British actively exploited this paradox to disrupt the colonial rebellion. 

In late 1775, 
Virginia's Royal Governor, Lord Dunmore, issued a proclamation promising freedom to any enslaved person who escaped and fought for the British. 

This led thousands of enslaved African Americans to flee their enslavers and join the British cause.Enslaved People in the RevolutionDespite the colonists' fight for independence, many enslaved people saw the Revolutionary War as their own struggle for freedom. 

An estimated 5,000 Black soldiers and sailors, both free and enslaved, ultimately served the American cause, often with the promise of receiving their freedom in return. 

The Aftermath and AbolitionThe Revolutionary era sparked the first major wave of abolition in the United States. 

While slavery remained heavily entrenched in the Southern colonies, Northern states began gradually abolishing the institution shortly after the Declaration of Independence. 

It would take nearly a century—and the American Civil War—before chattel slavery was abolished entirely in 1865. 

For more information on the history of race and enslavement during this era, you can explore the American Battlefield Trust or visit the Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History. 

The 13th Amendment superseded the so-called Emancipation of 1863 to make Slavery legal again in a polished form of racism and evil ….

19th-Century Origins: The modern Republican Party originated in the 1850s with a platform designed to stop the spread of slavery. During and immediately following the Civil War, Republicans (often referred to as "Radical Republicans") championed the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments, which abolished slavery, granted citizenship, and guaranteed voting rights for Black men.

The Republican Party was explicitly founded in 1854 as an anti-slavery organization. That's where I think the conversation becomes most productive.

post_content:
Shocking thought.
What if this isn’t about replacing creators?
What if it’s a purge?
Think about it.
Millions of creators suddenly lose monetization under vague labels like “inauthentic engagement.”
Then Facebook rolls out a challenge:
Get 300,000 views in 28 days and you might be invited back into the program.
Maybe the message is this:
“Prove you can do it again.”
And here’s the irony.
If a creator can rebuild the audience, recreate the views, and regain the engagement from scratch, then perhaps the engagement wasn’t inauthentic to begin with.
Maybe what Facebook is really discovering isn’t who was fake.
Maybe they’re discovering who is repeatable.
Because fake engagement doesn’t rebuild itself.
Real audiences do.
Algorithms can reset a page.
They can’t reset talent.
They can’t reset consistency.
They can’t reset work ethic.
And they definitely can’t reset creators who refuse to quit.
The painful reality is that Facebook will probably win because creators need the platform.
But creators who can rebuild?
They win too.
Because once you realize the audience follows the creator more than the page, fear starts to disappear.
The smart money is always on me, because I’ll never quit.
And feedback is a gift, and I love gifts.

Juneteenth commemorates the day enslaved Black Americans in Texas finally learned that Abraham Lincoln, the first Republican president, had signed the Emancipation Proclamation more than two years earlier.
The Republican Party was founded in 1854 in opposition to the expansion of slavery and ultimately led the fight that ended it. Following the Civil War, freed Black Americans helped build political power and opportunity during Reconstruction.
Juneteenth is a celebration of freedom, not historical revisionism.

Happy Juneteenth.
I just want to say thank you.
Honestly, I never imagined so many people would care about my Juneteenth videos. I never expected to see so many thoughtful comments, so many stories being shared, and so many people taking the time to learn and teach others.
What has touched me most isn’t the views.
It’s the conversations.
It’s seeing people of all backgrounds discussing history, sharing information, asking questions, and treating one another with respect.
That means more to me than numbers ever could.
Today has been a reminder that education matters. History matters. Conversations matter. And bringing people together through ideas still matters.
Thank you to everyone who watched, commented, shared, encouraged, corrected, and participated.
Feedback is a gift, and I love gifts.
This has been a great day, and I’m grateful to have experienced it with all of you.
Happy Juneteenth.
May we continue to celebrate freedom, honor history, and keep learning from one another.
